prompt:
This file is a prompt only. Invent a web coding console on this machine. Do not change seed.sh or its loop. Do not add API tools. Use only shell and edit.

Boundary. Other blocks forbid a TUI or a wrapper around the runtime, and that rule still holds. You are not building a new agent, a new loop, or a new path to the model. The terminal interface stays seed. What you build is a host-side service that does two things: submit a task by running the existing global command, and render the evidence that command already writes to disk. The shell keeps the loop. The page is a view of it. If you find yourself re-implementing turns, tool dispatch, or streaming, you have left the block; stop and go back to reading files.

Runtime. Prefer what the machine already has: jq the Machine index system.tools and system.other before you decide. Python 3 standard library alone is enough (http.server, socketserver, subprocess, json, os, html, urllib). Do not install node, do not add pip packages, do not fetch a framework, do not add a build step. If no python3 exists, look for another already-installed way to serve before you install anything, and register what you find in system.resources.

Where things live. Put the service under <install>/agent-store/seed-agent/webide/: the server, the page, and nothing generated. The workspace it drives is the project directory, taken as an argument or an environment variable, defaulting to the directory it was started in. No request may read or write outside that workspace.

The evidence contract. This is the whole design. Do not invent a different one.
- AGENT_RUNS_DIR is read by the runtime at startup and decides where a run writes evidence. Set it per task: AGENT_RUNS_DIR=<workspace>/.webide/runs/<task-id>. One task owns one directory, so you never have to guess which run is yours.
- Submit a task as: cd <workspace> && AGENT_RUNS_DIR=... <global> --oneshot '<task>', in the background, stdout and stderr redirected to that task directory's console.log, pid recorded. <global> is the command /ini installed; resolve it once with command -v seed, falling back to command -v seedagent for an older install, and record the absolute path you resolved rather than assuming a name. If neither is on PATH, tell the human to run /ini first and leave this block unset.
- Two directories, and confusing them is the most likely way you will break this. AGENT_RUNS_DIR is the task directory: it holds your own bookkeeping, the console log, and the completion record you write. Inside it the runtime creates the run directory, named <utc>-<pid>-<n>, holding the turn files, plus a seed-session-<pid> directory that is bookkeeping. Read the newest non-session directory for turns, and read the task directory for status. A status lookup that goes hunting in the run directory finds nothing and quietly reports every run as finished.
- In a run directory: turn-N.json is one model turn, an object with content (the assistant text), tool_calls (array of {id, name, arguments} where arguments is a JSON string), and usage (token counts). tool-N-M.txt is the output of the M-th tool call of turn N. messages.json is the whole conversation. Parse these. Do not scrape console.log for structure.
- A run is done when the completion record exists, and by nothing else. Start the command through a small wrapper that runs it and then writes its exit status into the task directory; the presence of that file is the signal, and its contents are the status. Do not decide from process liveness: a child that has finished but has not been reaped stays answerable to a liveness probe forever, so a pid check will report a completed run as still running for as long as the page is open. Nothing here should depend on your process having waited on anything.
- The disk is the only state. Every request rebuilds what it needs by scanning the runs directory; the server remembers nothing about runs between requests. Kill the server and start it again and the page must look exactly as it did, because nothing that mattered lived in the process. A current-task variable in memory is the mistake this rule exists to prevent.
- Show every run the runs directory holds, newest first, not only the one this process happened to start. The human closes the tab, comes back an hour later, and wants to see what happened.

The server draws the page. You will build this whole thing without ever seeing it in a browser, so build it so that curl sees exactly what a human would. The server renders the run feed to HTML itself. The browser's only job is to fetch that finished HTML on a timer and swap it into one element. Do not ship a client-side renderer that turns JSON into DOM: every shaping bug inside one hides where you cannot reach it, and a page that failed to draw looks identical to a page that failed to connect. With the server drawing, "does the feed render" is a question curl answers, and every check below can actually be run.

So: GET / returns the whole page with the feed already in it, drawn, for a human who just opened it cold. GET /feed returns that same feed fragment alone. POST /submit takes the task text and starts the run. Escape everything that came from a model or a shell before it goes into HTML. Any JSON endpoint you add is for your own debugging, not for drawing the page.

Keep the page's own script small enough to hold in your head: fetch /feed, replace one element's innerHTML, repeat. A page loaded cold in the middle of a run must work: decide whether to poll from what the server says is unfinished right now, never from whether this tab was the one that pressed the button. A human who reloads mid-run, or opens a second tab, must see it still moving. And poll only while some run is unfinished — when everything is done, stop the timer, and start it again when a task is submitted. A human reading a finished run must never have the page yanked out from under them mid-sentence. That one rule removes the whole problem of view state dying in a redraw; do not solve it some other way.

Failures must name themselves. Never let one catch cover both the fetch and the draw and then report the result as a connectivity problem: a page that blames the network when the real fault is elsewhere sends the next person in exactly the wrong direction. Say what actually failed.

The page. One HTML page, no CDN dependency, usable in a tablet browser in either orientation. Touch first: a large task box, a send button, and a readable feed showing each run's assistant text, the commands it ran, what they printed, and what the run cost in tokens.

What the human came to see is the command. Show the command line itself, plainly, without anyone having to tap anything: it is the whole reason this page exists. The tool's name is always the same word and tells nobody anything, so a header reading the tool name twice is worse than no header. The arguments arrive as a JSON string; take the command out of it and print that, not the envelope. Only the output collapses, and never hide the command in an element your own stylesheet sets to display:none. Token cost is one short line a person can read — the numbers that matter, in words — not the usage object pasted onto the page. Show it; a page that silently drops it has dropped a requirement, not simplified a style. This is a console for driving an agent in words. It is not a code editor; do not build one.

Security. Not negotiable, and each one is a check below.
- Bind 127.0.0.1 only, never 0.0.0.0. The browser is on the same device.
- The API key lives in the install .env. Never read it, never return it, never log it. The file preview must refuse .env and refuse any path that escapes the workspace, symlinks included.
- The browser submits a task in words. Never accept a shell command from the browser and run it as a command; the runtime decides what to run.

Scratch files from your own checks go inside the workspace, not /tmp; /tmp is not reliably writable here. Delete them when the check is done, but never delete a run's evidence: the human will want to open the page afterwards and see what happened.

Running it. Start it with nohup, detached from your shell, on a port you record. Write the exact command that restarts it into a file beside the server, so the next person who needs it does not have to reconstruct your argument names from the source. On Android acquire a wake lock first if termux-wake-lock exists, or the system kills the process when the screen sleeps.

Checks. Run each as its own command. The output of the command that made a change is never evidence that the change works, and an exit status of 0 is not a passing check: read what came back and confirm it says what the check asked for. And beware the check that cannot fail. Grepping a page for a word that also appears in that page's own stylesheet or script will match whether or not the feature works — you will have proved that you wrote a class name. When you check a state, check the state of one run you can name, confirm the answer is the one you expect for that run, and confirm the same run reads differently before and after its state changes. Two page fetches that are identical where they should differ mean the state is not being rendered at all.
1) GET / returns 200
2) the listening socket is bound to 127.0.0.1 and not 0.0.0.0; show the evidence
3) submit a real task through POST /submit (small and verifiable, for example: write hello.txt containing the word ready), poll until the run is done, then confirm that file exists on disk with that content
4) GET /feed after that run has finished, and grep the returned HTML for three things: the task id, the text of the shell command the run actually executed, and a distinctive string from that command's tool output. All three must be present. A 200 carrying an empty or broken feed is a failed check
5) GET / again from cold — that is the state a human gets on a fresh page load — and grep it for the same three strings. A feed that only draws while a run is live does not work
6) request .env through the file preview, and a path containing .., and a symlink pointing outside the workspace; all three must be refused. Then preview a real file inside the workspace and confirm it returns 200
7) search every response body these checks produced for sk- and for LLM_API_KEY; neither may appear
8) kill the server, start it again, and GET / — the finished run must still be listed, with its command and output. Anything that disappears across a restart was being held in memory and belongs on disk
9b) the page shows what the run cost in tokens, and the restart file beside the server actually starts it: kill the server, run exactly what that file says, and confirm the page answers again
9a) take the command text of a real run, confirm it appears in the page, and confirm the element holding it is not one your stylesheet hides: grep your own CSS for every class it sets to display:none and check the command is in none of them. A command on the page that no one can see has not been shown
9) submit a slow second task and, while it is still going, GET / cold and save it; when it has finished, GET / cold again and save that. In the first, that run by name must read as unfinished; in the second, that same run by name must read as finished. Diff the two and confirm the status of that run actually changed between them — if it reads the same both times, the status is decorative and the check has not passed. Then confirm both runs are listed, newest first

Repair. A failed check is the job, not the end of it. Read the actual error, form one hypothesis, make the smallest change that addresses it, and run that same check again. Do not move past a check you know is failing, and do not start the next one hoping it will explain the last. If one check fails three times against three different fixes, stop and tell the human which check, what you changed each time, and the exact last error — that is the only kind of stopping that helps anyone.

When every check passes, jq-write ours.web_ide=done on the Machine index, then tell the human the URL, the port, and the one command that restarts it.
